{
  "title": "When Do Code Semantics Help? Trace-Supervised SFT for Code Behavior Prediction vs. Generation",
  "core_problem": "\"Do Code Semantics Help?\" (EMNLP Findings 2025, arXiv 2509.11686) concluded that execution trace-based SFT provides limited benefit for Code LLMs, finding it fails to improve code synthesis in 7/9 configurations and yields inconsistent results for CRUXEval reasoning tasks. However, all tasks studied require generating exact outputs — complete programs, precise I/O values, or repaired code. We ask: does trace SFT help for code behavior prediction — tasks with constrained output spaces where the model predicts a verdict about code execution behavior (pass/fail, correct/incorrect, buggy/clean) rather than generating code or exact values? Binary/categorical prediction is fundamentally simpler than generation, and the overconfidence-without-correctness phenomenon that harms generation (\"Do Code Semantics Help?\" Table 7: trace SFT boosts prediction confidence without increasing correctness) may actually benefit classification by sharpening decision boundaries. This distinction — verdict prediction vs. open generation — has not been systematically investigated.",
  "opportunity": "Three converging lines of evidence suggest trace SFT may help for behavior prediction despite failing for generation. First, SemCoder (NeurIPS 2024) demonstrates that trace-supervised training teaches genuine behavioral understanding (63.6% CRUXEval-I vs. 50.3% for Code Llama 34B at same scale). Second, ExecVerify (arXiv 2603.11226, 2026) shows execution-grounded RL enables 7B models to match 32B models on code reasoning benchmarks, demonstrating that execution awareness is a learnable capability. Third, \"Code Execution as Grounded Supervision\" (EMNLP 2025) demonstrates that execution-derived chain-of-thought transfers across reasoning domains. Yet nobody has tested whether this learned behavioral understanding helps for binary code assessment tasks specifically. The practical stakes are high: automated patch correctness assessment (APCA) plateaus at ~88% accuracy (ComPass: 88.35%, Historian: 88.4%) using purely static features, test outcome prediction is increasingly critical for efficient CI/CD, and bug detection accuracy determines triage quality. A systematic study resolving when trace SFT helps — across a spectrum from binary verdicts through constrained prediction to open generation — would both advance NLP understanding of code semantics and unlock practical applications. The study design ensures publishable value regardless of outcome: if trace SFT helps for verdicts, we identify a new capability; if it doesn't, we strengthen and extend the \"Do Code Semantics Help?\" negative finding to a broader task space.",
  "landscape": "Trace SFT for Code LLMs: \"Do Code Semantics Help?\" (EMNLP Findings 2025, arXiv 2509.11686) is the central prior work. Testing five trace representations (Scratchpad, NExT, SemCoder, CodeExecutor, Concise) across DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, and Gemma2-9B, they found trace SFT fails for code synthesis (7/9 configs), yields marginal gains for program repair (+0.3–1.4 pts with SemCoder only), and shows inconsistent CRUXEval results. Crucially, all their tasks are generative — no binary classification or verdict tasks were evaluated. SemCoder (arXiv 2406.01006, NeurIPS 2024) trains on monologue-style NL execution descriptions and achieves strong CRUXEval gains, showing trace training CAN teach behavioral understanding. Execution Tuning (E.T., arXiv 2503.05703, 2025) achieves ~80% on CRUXEval-O with dynamic scratchpads but requires traces at inference time — we aim to internalize this capability via SFT so no traces are needed at inference. ExecVerify (arXiv 2603.11226, 2026) uses white-box RL rewards from execution traces, enabling 7B ≈ 32B on reasoning benchmarks — but uses RL (we use SFT only, lower compute). \"Code Execution as Grounded Supervision\" (arXiv 2506.10343, EMNLP 2025) extracts verifiable CoT from code execution for general reasoning — complementary but applied to reasoning transfer, not code-specific verdict tasks. Self-Execution Simulation (arXiv 2604.03253, 2026) trains on NL traces + RL for competitive programming self-verification (+5.5% via best-of-k), but is limited to single-file code generation verification, not systematic behavior prediction.\n\nAutomated Patch Correctness Assessment (APCA): ComPass (arXiv 2602.07561, 2026) achieves 88.35% accuracy on Defects4J via contrastive learning on BERT representations — purely static. Historian (arXiv 2603.00649, 2026) achieves 88.4% accuracy with 95.0% coverage by comparing patches against historically validated fixes — also static, with a different inductive bias (pattern matching vs. behavioral reasoning). APSG/Graph-LoRA (arXiv 2505.02629, 2025) reaches 85.8–96.8% via attributed semantic graphs + LLaMA3 fine-tuning. RePaCA (arXiv 2507.22580, 2025) uses reasoning LLMs with generic CoT at 83.1% — our trace-supervised CoT is grounded in actual execution rather than generic reasoning. LLM4PatchCorrect (TSE 2024, IEEE 10.1109/TSE.2024.3452252) is the closest existing work: it uses execution traces as in-context learning input for StarCoder, achieving 84.4% accuracy. The key distinction from our work is ICL vs. SFT: LLM4PatchCorrect requires traces at inference time (expensive), while we internalize trace reasoning via SFT (traces needed only during training). Shibboleth (ISSTA 2022) achieves 88.7% but requires test execution at inference. APPT (TSE 2024) uses BERT+LSTM at 79.7%. No existing APCA method uses trace-supervised SFT.\n\nBenchmarks: CRUXEval (arXiv 2401.03065, ICML 2024) provides 800 Python functions for execution prediction (I/O tasks). LiveCodeBench (arXiv 2403.07974) offers contamination-free code evaluation including test output prediction. DebugBench (2024) has 4,253 instances across C++/Java/Python with 18 bug types. CrossCodeEval (arXiv 2310.11248, NeurIPS 2023) evaluates cross-file code completion across 4 languages. Defects4J provides 2,274 labeled patches for APCA evaluation.\n\nKey gap: No prior work has systematically compared trace SFT effectiveness across the verdict–prediction–generation task spectrum. \"Do Code Semantics Help?\" covers prediction and generation but omits verdict tasks entirely. LLM4PatchCorrect explores traces for APCA but via ICL, not SFT. SemCoder and E.T. show trace training builds behavioral understanding but don't test whether it helps binary classification. We fill this gap.",
  "approach": "We conduct a systematic empirical study of trace-supervised SFT across three code task categories, directly extending \"Do Code Semantics Help?\" (EMNLP Findings 2025) to verdict tasks.\n\n**Task Taxonomy.** We define three categories by output space constraint: (1) Verdict tasks — binary/categorical judgments about code behavior: patch correctness (correct/overfitting), test outcome prediction (pass/fail), bug detection (buggy/clean). (2) Constrained prediction — generating specific values from a small output space: CRUXEval-O (output prediction), LiveCodeBench test output prediction. (3) Open generation — producing arbitrary code: HumanEval, MBPP, CrossCodeEval. Our hypothesis: trace SFT effectiveness increases as output space narrows, because binary classification requires only approximate behavioral understanding while generation demands exact simulation.\n\n**Data Construction & Trace Collection (~35h wall-clock, CPU-bound, parallelizable).**\n• APCA-Defects4J: 2,274 labeled patches (1,169 correct, 1,105 overfitting). Apply each patch, run relevant tests (~10–20/patch) with JUnit instrumentation capturing variable states at assertion points, exception types, and loop counts. Augment with PraPatch (1,988 patches). ~30h wall-clock on 4-core machine.\n• TestVerdict-HumanEval/MBPP: Generate 10 solutions per problem using Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct (mix of correct and incorrect). Run each against test cases with Python sys.settrace instrumentation. ~664 problems × 10 solutions = ~6,640 (solution, test, trace, pass/fail) examples. ~3h wall-clock.\n• BugDetect-DebugBench: Take 4,253 buggy programs + their correct versions. Run both on LeetCode test cases with trace instrumentation. ~8,500 (program, trace, buggy/clean + bug_type) examples. ~2h wall-clock.\n• CRUXEval traces: 800 Python functions, instrument execution with sys.settrace. ~1h wall-clock.\n\n**Trace Abstraction (GPU, ~15–20h H100).** Convert raw traces to concise NL execution descriptions using Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct. Two formats: (1) SemCoder-style full NL monologues (for direct comparison with \"Do Code Semantics Help?\"), (2) Assessment-optimized concise format: variable snapshots at assertion points only, exception summaries (type + message), loop compression (first/last + count), collection summaries (size + boundaries). The concise format directly addresses token-budget exhaustion identified by Debugging CWM (arXiv 2602.07672).\n\n**Trace-Supervised SFT (GPU, ~60–70h H100).** Fine-tune two base models with LoRA (rank 32, alpha 64):\n• Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct (primary, strong code model)\n• DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct (for direct comparison with \"Do Code Semantics Help?\" which used this model)\n\nTraining format by task type:\n• Verdict tasks: input = (code + test + instruction) → output = (NL trace reasoning + verdict label). The model learns to generate execution reasoning as chain-of-thought grounded in real traces before predicting the verdict.\n• CRUXEval-O: input = (function + input value) → output = (NL trace reasoning + predicted output). Matches \"Do Code Semantics Help?\" protocol for direct comparison.\n• Generation tasks: standard SFT without trace supervision (replication of DCSH setup).\n\nWe train separate LoRA adapters for each task category to isolate trace SFT's task-specific effects, plus a multi-task model trained on all verdict tasks jointly.\n\n**Go/No-Go Pilot (GPU, ~5h H100).** Before committing full resources, we run a rapid pilot: train on 20% of APCA-Defects4J data, evaluate on held-out fold. If trace SFT shows ≥2% improvement over no-trace baseline, proceed with full experiments. If not, we shift emphasis to the negative-result framing and invest more in analysis of WHY traces don't help.\n\n**Evaluation Protocol.**\n• Verdict tasks: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (10,000 resamples). McNemar's test for pairwise comparison with baselines (ComPass, LLM4PatchCorrect, Historian). For APCA: 5-fold cross-validation matching ComPass's protocol; complementarity analysis with ComPass showing error-type overlap; simple majority-vote ensemble targeting >90% accuracy.\n• CRUXEval-O: pass@1, matching \"Do Code Semantics Help?\" protocol exactly for controlled comparison.\n• LiveCodeBench test output prediction: pass@1 on problems after model training cutoff (contamination-free).\n• Generation tasks (HumanEval, MBPP, CrossCodeEval): pass@1 / exact match / edit similarity, replicating DCSH to confirm trace SFT doesn't help for generation.\n\n**Core Analyses.**\n(1) Task-spectrum analysis: Plot trace SFT improvement (Δ accuracy/pass@1) vs. output space constraint across all tasks. Test the hypothesis that benefit decreases as output space expands.\n(2) Confidence-correctness analysis: Replicate DCSH Table 7 analysis for verdict tasks. We predict that the overconfidence effect is BENEFICIAL for binary classification (sharper sigmoid boundaries) but harmful for generation (confidently wrong outputs).\n(3) APCA complementarity: Error-type analysis showing our method catches behaviorally incorrect patches that static methods (ComPass, Historian) miss, and vice versa. Ensemble analysis.\n(4) Ablations: trace granularity (SemCoder vs. concise), LoRA rank (16/32/64), training data size curves.\n(5) Differentiation from LLM4PatchCorrect: head-to-head comparison showing SFT internalization vs. ICL context — our method requires no traces at inference, while achieving competitive or better accuracy.\n\n**Scope Limitations.** We focus on function-level bugs and single-file programs, explicitly acknowledging that scaling to repository-level multi-file tasks is an open challenge. For DebugBench, we evaluate Python and Java subsets. For Defects4J, we characterize accuracy degradation across bug complexity categories (single-hunk vs. multi-hunk). We do not include SWE-bench Verified due to confirmed test quality issues (OpenAI audit finding 59.4% flawed tests in audited subset).\n\n**Differentiation from key related work:** vs. \"Do Code Semantics Help?\": we extend their study to verdict tasks (binary/categorical classification), a task category they did not evaluate, and test whether the overconfidence effect they identified is beneficial for classification. vs. LLM4PatchCorrect: SFT internalization (no traces at inference) vs. ICL (requires traces at inference). vs. SemCoder: we apply trace-supervised models to downstream verdict tasks rather than evaluating on generation benchmarks. vs. ExecVerify: SFT-only (lower compute, more accessible) vs. RL with execution rewards. vs. Self-Execution Simulation: systematic multi-task evaluation across the task spectrum vs. single-task verification. vs. Historian: behavioral reasoning via learned execution simulation vs. pattern matching against historical patches.",

## Reviewer feedback (round 3)
Issues: ["MODERATE: Missing competitor — TraceMind/TracePile (arXiv 2510.23629, NeurIPS 2025) trains on 2.6M execution trace samples across LLaMA 3, LLaMA 3.1, Qwen-2.5, Qwen-2.5 Coder and evaluates on 20 benchmarks including CRUXEval. While it targets generation/reasoning (not verdict tasks), it is the largest-scale trace SFT effort and must be discussed in the landscape. It strengthens your argument (even massive-scale trace SFT targets generation, not classification) but omitting it is a gap a reviewer would catch.", "MODERATE: The overconfidence-helps-classification hypothesis is the most intellectually interesting contribution but remains purely speculative. The proposal should design a concrete experiment to test it: measure Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Brier score before/after trace SFT for both verdict tasks and generation tasks. If trace SFT improves calibration for binary tasks while worsening it for generation, that's a strong finding. Without quantitative calibration analysis, the hypothesis is hand-waving.", "MODERATE: RepoBench is absent from evaluation despite being explicitly listed in the user's required benchmarks ('SWE-bench Verified, HumanEval/MBPP, CrossCodeEval, RepoBench, DebugBench, CodeContests'). While SWE-bench exclusion is well-justified and CodeContests exclusion is reasonable for a verdict-focused study, RepoBench (repo-level code completion) should either be included or its exclusion explicitly justified.", "MODERATE: The contribution sits ambiguously between 'method paper' and 'empirical study.' The user explicitly requested 'METHOD ONLY — propose new training methods.' To fully satisfy this, the assessment-optimized concise trace format (assertion-point snapshots, loop compression, collection summaries) should be elevated from an implementation detail to a first-class contribution — a novel trace representation designed specifically for classification tasks. Compare it systematically against SemCoder/NExT/Scratchpad/Concise formats from DCSH with per-task-type ablations. This turns 'applying method A to task B' into 'designing representation C optimized for task category B.'", "MINOR: The APCA ensemble result (trace SFT + ComPass targeting >90% accuracy) is potentially the strongest practical headline but is currently buried. If achievable, it should be positioned as a primary contribution: breaking the ~88% APCA plateau via complementary behavioral + static analysis approaches. This concretely addresses 'what does the NLP community gain from this study?'", "MINOR: FGIT: Fault-Guided Fine-Tuning (arXiv 2503.16913, ASE 2025) uses correct/incorrect code signal during SFT with dynamic loss weighting. While technically different (loss reweighting for generation, not classification), it occupies a conceptually adjacent space and should be briefly discussed to show awareness of the broader 'using correctness signals in code SFT' landscape."]
Feedback: This is a well-crafted proposal that has improved dramatically across rounds. The gap is independently verified as genuine, references are accurate, and feasibility is sound. The idea is close to passing but needs targeted improvements to reach the 4.0 threshold:

**1. Elevate the concise trace format as a novel method contribution.** Currently it reads as an implementation choice. Reframe it: you're proposing an 'assessment-optimized trace representation' — assertion-point variable snapshots + exception summaries + loop compression + collection boundaries — specifically designed for verdict tasks where full execution simulation is unnecessary. Run systematic ablations comparing this format against all 5 DCSH trace representations (Scratchpad, NExT, SemCoder, CodeExecutor, Concise) on verdict tasks specifically. This is your METHOD contribution, not just 'SFT on traces for classification.'

**2. Operationalize the overconfidence hypothesis.** Add ECE (Expected Calibration Error) and reliability diagrams to your evaluation protocol. Concretely measure: (a) prediction confidence distributions before/after trace SFT on verdict vs generation tasks; (b) calibration curves showing whether trace SFT sharpens decision boundaries for binary tasks; (c) contrast with DCSH Table 7 analysis. This transforms a speculative hypothesis into a testable, quantitative finding.

**3. Add TraceMind/TracePile (arXiv 2510.23629, NeurIPS 2025) to related work.** Position it as: 'Even at 2.6M-sample scale, trace SFT has only been applied to generative tasks — we test whether the verdict/classification regime responds differently.'

**4. Strengthen the APCA ensemble as headline result.** If trace SFT provides complementary error patterns to ComPass/Historian (behavioral vs. static analysis), a simple majority-vote ensemble breaking 90% accuracy would be a concrete, practically meaningful result. Position this prominently.

**5. Either include RepoBench or explicitly justify exclusion.** Since it's in the user's required benchmark list, at minimum note why verdict-task evaluation on RepoBench is infeasible (it's a code completion benchmark, not a verdict benchmark).

With these changes, the novelty score rises (novel trace representation + quantified calibration finding) and impact improves (concrete >90% APCA ensemble + calibration insight). This would bring the average above 4.0 for a solid Findings paper.

## Instructions
- Think in two phases: FIRST reconsider the problem framing (core_problem / opportunity / landscape) if the reviewer flagged issues there, THEN revise the method (approach / resource_estimate / key_references). Do not jump straight to fixing the method if the underlying problem framing needs correction.
- Address each issue specifically.

## 深度调研要求（每一轮修订都必须执行）

不要简单地'打补丁'——每一轮修订都是重新审视和深化这个 idea 的机会。

1. **深度搜索**：针对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，建议用 2-3 种不同的搜索查询调研。
   - 搜索最新的相关论文（arXiv, conference proceedings）
   - 搜索 benchmark/leaderboard 确认当前 SOTA
   - 搜索可能遗漏的相关工作和 concurrent work

2. **深度阅读**：用 WebFetch 实际阅读找到的关键论文的 abstract 和方法部分，
   不要只依赖搜索摘要。形成你自己对领域现状的独立判断。

3. **深度思考**：在修订之前，先独立思考以下问题：
   - 这个 idea 的核心假设是否仍然成立？
   - reviewer 的批评是否揭示了更深层的问题？
   - 有没有更好的 framing 或 approach 来解决同一个核心问题？
   - 修订后的 idea 相比上一版有什么本质性的改进？

4. **避免表面修订**：如果你发现自己只是在换措辞或补充细节而没有实质改进，
   考虑是否需要 major revision 或 pivot。反复的 minor fix 不会拯救一个根基有问题的 idea。

## 针对 Review 意见的定向搜索

对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，执行以下搜索流程：

1. **如果 reviewer 说'已有类似工作'**：
   - 搜索 reviewer 提到的论文，用 WebFetch 实际阅读
   - 搜索该论文的 cited-by，找到后续跟进工作
   - 明确你的 idea 与这些工作的差异化点——如果差异化不够，必须 pivot

2. **如果 reviewer 说'SOTA 过时'**：
   - 用 Papers With Code 查看当前排行榜
   - 搜索过去 6 个月的最新方法
   - 更新你的 landscape 和 baseline

3. **如果 reviewer 说'可行性有问题'**：
   - 搜索类似规模实验的实际成本和时间线
   - 搜索 GitHub 上是否有可复用的实现
   - 搜索相关数据集/模型的可获取性

4. **如果 reviewer 说'novelty 不足'**：
   - 对核心方法尽量做 3-5 种不同关键词组合的搜索
   - 搜索相邻领域是否有类似思路
   - 如果确实 novelty 不足，考虑 major revision 或 pivot

- Use WebSearch to find updated information if the reviewer flagged outdated claims.
- You have full freedom in how much to change:
  - Minor fix: if only specific details are wrong, correct them and keep everything else.
  - Major revision: if the approach is fundamentally flawed but the core problem is valid, you may redesign the approach entirely.
  - Pivot: if the reviewer's feedback reveals that the core problem itself is invalid (e.g., the gap no longer exists), you may propose a RELATED but substantially different idea that builds on the same research area. This is preferred over forcing a doomed idea to pass review.
- The output replaces the original idea (same tracking ID). Whether you make a small tweak or a full pivot, output a COMPLETE JSON object with ALL fields filled.
- In the output JSON, include a "change_type" field with one of: "minor", "major", or "pivot" to indicate the scope of your changes.
- Output the revised idea as a COMPLETE JSON object (same schema as original, plus "change_type").

## Overview

FGIT (Fault-Guided Fine-Tuning) is a novel fine-tuning technique that enhances LLMs' code generation by extracting multi-granularity (line/token-level) differences between correct and incorrect yet similar implementations to identify error-sensitive segments, and dynamically prioritizing those segments during training via dynamic loss weighting.

## Problem It Addresses

LLMs fine-tuned with standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) sometimes generate plausible-looking but functionally incorrect code variants. This issue likely stems from the limitation of standard SFT, which treats all tokens equally during optimization and fails to emphasize the error-sensitive segments—specific code differences between correct implementations and similar incorrect variants.

Through extensive experiments on seven LLMs across three widely-used benchmarks, the method achieves an average relative improvement of 6.9% on pass@1, with some enhanced 6.7B LLMs outperforming closed-source models like GPT-3.5-Turbo.

## Overview of ECE

Expected Calibration Error (ECE) is a widely used evaluation measure for confidence calibration that measures how well a model's estimated probabilities match the observed probabilities by taking a weighted average over the absolute difference between average accuracy and average confidence.

## ECE in Code Language Models

Recent research (2025) has specifically examined ECE for code language models. For code completion tasks with language models, rescaling can improve ECE from an average of 0.32 to 0.03. Additionally, both GPT-3.5 and CODEX show positive skill scores and low ECE for certain confidence measures, though they are inconsistent after normalization.

## Binary Classification

For binary classification specifically, ECE measures how well a model's estimated probabilities match the true probabilities by taking a weighted average over the absolute difference between accuracy and confidence, and the measure involves splitting the data into M equally spaced bins.

## Known Limitations and Recent Developments

The value of ECE depends on the choice of bin number and bin boundaries, with too few bins able to hide discrepancies while too many lead to high variance and unstable estimates, and small changes in model output can cause large, discontinuous jumps in the metric.

Recent work from 2025-2026 has proposed alternatives and improvements. SmoothECE uses kernel smoothing with a reflected Gaussian kernel to replace hard binning, yielding a continuous, stable calibration error estimate that avoids bin-boundary artifacts.

## "Calibration and Correctness of Language Models for Code" - ICSE 2025

The paper is authored by Claudio Spiess, David Gros, Kunal Suresh Pai, Michael Pradel, Rafiqul Rabin, Amin Alipour, Susmit Jha, Prem Devanbu, and Toufique Ahmed, and was presented at ICSE 2025 Research Track.

### Key Contributions

The researchers developed a framework for evaluating the calibration of code-generating models and found that generative code models are not well-calibrated out of the box. They then showed how calibration can be improved using standard methods such as Platt scaling, and evaluated the applicability and generalizability of Platt scaling in Software Engineering.

### Main Focus

The paper addresses how outputs can be associated with a confidence measure; if this confidence measure is strongly associated with likelihood of correctness, then the model is said to be well-calibrated, and this confidence measure can serve as a basis for rational graduated decision making on how much review and care is needed.

### Practical Implications

A well-calibrated confidence measure would support rational risk-management in the development process, enabling policies where code with high confidence could be reviewed lightly, medium confidence suggestions should be reviewed more carefully, and low confidence suggestions should be rejected or the prompt adjusted.

The paper also addresses the challenge that calibration has so far been studied in mostly non-generative (e.g., classification) settings, especially in Software Engineering.

## "Calibration and Correctness of Language Models for Code" - ICSE 2025

The paper is authored by Claudio Spiess, David Gros, Kunal Suresh Pai, Michael Pradel, Rafiqul Rabin, Amin Alipour, Susmit Jha, Prem Devanbu, and Toufique Ahmed, and was presented at ICSE 2025 Research Track.

### Key Contributions

The researchers developed a framework for evaluating the calibration of code-generating models and found that generative code models are not well-calibrated out of the box. They then showed how calibration can be improved using standard methods such as Platt scaling, and evaluated the applicability and generalizability of Platt scaling in Software Engineering.

### Main Focus

The paper addresses how outputs can be associated with a confidence measure; if this confidence measure is strongly associated with likelihood of correctness, then the model is said to be well-calibrated, and this confidence measure can serve as a basis for rational graduated decision making on how much review and care is needed.

### Practical Implications

A well-calibrated confidence measure would support rational risk-management in the development process, enabling policies where code with high confidence could be reviewed lightly, medium confidence suggestions should be reviewed more carefully, and low confidence suggestions should be rejected or the prompt adjusted.

The paper also addresses the challenge that calibration has so far been studied in mostly non-generative (e.g., classification) settings, especially in Software Engineering.

# FGIT: Fault-Guided Fine-Tuning for Code Generation

## Full Abstract

"Modern instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress in code generation. However, these LLMs fine-tuned with standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) sometimes generate plausible-looking but functionally incorrect code variants. This issue likely stems from the limitation of standard SFT, which treats all tokens equally during optimization and fails to emphasize the error-sensitive segments-specific code differences between correct implementations and similar incorrect variants. To address this problem, we propose Fault-Guided Fine-Tuning (FGIT), a novel fine-tuning technique that enhances LLMs' code generation by (1) extracting multi-granularity (line/token-level) differences between correct and incorrect yet similar implementations to identify error-sensitive segments, and (2) dynamically prioritizing those segments during training via dynamic loss weighting. Through extensive experiments on seven LLMs across three widely-used benchmarks, our method achieves an average relative improvement of 6.9% on pass@1 with some enhanced 6.7B LLMs outperforming closed-source models, e.g., GPT-3.5-Turbo. Furthermore, our fine-tuning technique demonstrates strong generalization with performance improvements ranging from 3.8% to 19.1% across diverse instruction-tuned LLMs, and our ablation studies confirm the contributions of different granularities of differences and hyperparameters."

## Core Method

FGIT employs two primary techniques: (1) identifying critical code segments by comparing correct and incorrect implementations at multiple granularities (line and token levels), and (2) applying dynamic loss weighting to emphasize these error-prone areas during training.

## Models & Benchmarks

- **Models tested:** Seven instruction-tuned LLMs (including 6.7B variants)
- **Benchmarks:** Three widely-used code generation benchmarks
- **Comparisons:** Outperforms GPT-3.5-Turbo on some metrics

## Task Scope

This work focuses **exclusively on code generation**, not code classification.

## Key Innovation

The primary innovation is dynamic loss weighting applied to fault-sensitive code segments, enabling the model to concentrate training emphasis on regions most likely to contain errors.

## Overconfidence and Fine-Tuning

LLMs' extensive prior knowledge, while enabling remarkable few-shot generalization, paradoxically causes their poor calibration in fine-tuning paradigms.

### How Fine-Tuning Affects Calibration

The research reveals nuanced effects depending on the type of data:

**Known vs. Unknown Data:** Data aligned with the model's prior knowledge (known data) tend to cause overconfidence, while data exhibiting knowledge bias (unknown data) contribute to better calibration. The model quickly assimilates known data, leading to continued confidence growth even after accuracy plateaus.

**Different Fine-Tuning Methods:** Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) yields well-calibrated confidence through maximum-likelihood estimation, whereas reinforcement learning methods (PPO, GRPO) and DPO induce overconfidence via reward exploitation.

### Impact on Binary Prediction

For binary classification specifically, fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) often exhibit overconfidence, particularly when trained on small datasets, resulting in poor calibration and inaccurate uncertainty estimates.

### Solutions Being Developed

Recent work proposes various approaches: In the calibratable regime, calibration-aware fine-tuning approaches can achieve proper calibration without compromising LLMs' performance. Additionally, post-RL SFT with self-distillation can restore confidence reliability in RL-trained models.

The consensus is that while fine-tuning can hurt calibration through overconfidence, targeted calibration-aware approaches during fine-tuning can help restore proper alignment between confidence and accuracy.

# TRACED: Execution-aware Pre-training for Source Code

## Full Abstract
"Most existing pre-trained language models for source code focus on learning the static code text, typically augmented with static code structures (abstract syntax tree, dependency graphs, etc.). However, program semantics will not be fully exposed before the real execution. Without an understanding of the program execution, statically pre-trained models fail to comprehensively capture the dynamic code properties, such as the branch coverage and the runtime variable values, and they are consequently less effective at code understanding tasks, such as retrieving semantic clones and detecting software vulnerabilities. To close the gap between the static nature of language models and the dynamic characteristics of programs, we introduce TRACED, an execution-aware pre-training strategy for source code. Specifically, we pre-train code language models with a combination of source code, executable inputs, and corresponding execution traces. Our goal is to teach code models the complicated execution logic during the pre-training, enabling the model to statically estimate the dynamic code properties without repeatedly executing code during task-specific fine-tuning. To illustrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach, we fine-tune and evaluate TRACED on three downstream tasks: static execution estimation, clone retrieval, and vulnerability detection. The empirical results show that TRACED relatively improves the statically pre-trained code models by 12.4% for complete execution path prediction and by 25.2% for runtime variable value predictions. TRACED also significantly outperforms statically pre-trained models in clone retrieval and vulnerability detection across four public benchmarks."

## Specific Results
The paper does **not provide exact numerical results** for vulnerability detection or clone retrieval performance. It only states TRACED "significantly outperforms statically pre-trained models" across both tasks but lacks detailed metrics.

## Execution Traces for Classification
Yes, TRACED demonstrates that execution traces improve code classification—the model learns dynamic properties to enhance performance on classification-oriented tasks like vulnerability detection and clone retrieval.

## Overview

Code World Models (CWMs) are language models trained to simulate program execution by predicting explicit runtime state after every executed command. This execution-based world modeling enables internal verification within the model, offering an alternative to natural language chain-of-thought reasoning.

The paper identifies two dominant failure regimes in CWMs:

The researchers study CWMs from two complementary perspectives: local semantic execution and long-horizon state tracking. This dual-lens approach helps understand both immediate semantic execution errors and compounding errors over longer sequences.

## ExecRepoBench Overview

ExecRepoBench is a repository-level benchmark created alongside the instruction corpora Repo-Instruct to improve the functionality of open-source large language models (LLMs) in real-world coding scenarios that involve complex interdependencies across multiple files.

## Benchmark Composition

ExecRepoBench is created with repository-level unit tests to verify the correctness of completion code, comprised of 1.2K samples from 50 active Python repositories.

## Execution Traces and Evaluation

Similar to in-file benchmarks HumanEval/MBPP, the evaluation employs the Pass@k metric based on executable results to get the reliability evaluation results. The evaluation includes standard metrics like edit similarity (ES) for string-based preference and the Pass@k metric, where Pass@1 assesses whether the proposed code passes all unit tests, emphasizing the necessity of execution validation.

A multi-level grammar-based completion methodology is presented that is conditioned on the abstract syntax tree to mask code fragments at various logical units (e.g. statements, expressions, and functions). Based on the search results, I found comprehensive information about ExecRepoBench:

## ExecRepoBench Overview

ExecRepoBench is a repository-level benchmark created alongside the instruction corpora Repo-Instruct to improve the functionality of open-source large language models (LLMs) in real-world coding scenarios that involve complex interdependencies across multiple files.

## Benchmark Composition

ExecRepoBench is created with repository-level unit tests to verify the correctness of completion code, comprised of 1.2K samples from 50 active Python repositories.

## Execution Traces and Evaluation

Similar to in-file benchmarks HumanEval/MBPP, the evaluation employs the Pass@k metric based on executable results to get the reliability evaluation results. The evaluation includes standard metrics like edit similarity (ES) for string-based preference and the Pass@k metric, where Pass@1 assesses whether the proposed code passes all unit tests, emphasizing the necessity of execution validation.

## Multi-level Code Completion

A multi-level grammar-based completion methodology is presented that is conditioned on the abstract syntax tree to mask code fragments at various logical units (e.g. statements, expressions, and functions). The researchers utilized an abstract syntax tree (AST) to enhance the completion tasks at various granularity levels: expression-level, statement-level, function-level, and class-level.

## Recent Development

The paper was published in December 2024 (arXiv:2412.11990), and the open-source LLM with 7B parameters was fine-tuned on Repo-Instruct to produce Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct-C, which is rigorously evaluated against existing benchmarks, including MultiPL-E and ExecRepoBench, and consistently outperforms prior baselines across all programming languages.

**Method Contribution: VOTA Trace Representation.** Existing trace formats (Scratchpad, NExT, SemCoder, CodeExecutor, Concise from DCSH; CoE from TracePile) are designed for full execution simulation — capturing every variable state, every loop iteration, every line of execution. This is appropriate for generation tasks that require exact output prediction, but excessive for verdict tasks where the model only needs to determine whether code behaves correctly. VOTA is designed around the principle that verdict tasks require only decision-relevant execution states:
• Assertion-point variable snapshots: Capture variable states only at test assertion points and function entry/exit boundaries, not at every line. For a test with 5 assertions, this yields ~5 state snapshots vs. potentially hundreds for full-trace formats.
• Exception summaries: Type + message + triggering line only, not full stack traces. Captures the diagnostic signal while discarding syntactic noise.
• Loop compression: First iteration state, last iteration state, iteration count, and any iteration where state diverges from the pattern. This directly addresses the token-budget exhaustion failure mode identified by Debugging CWM (arXiv 2602.07672).
• Collection boundaries: For lists/dicts/sets, capture size + first/last elements + any elements referenced in assertions, not full contents.
• Behavioral delta format: For patch correctness tasks, VOTA additionally captures a behavioral diff — how the patched code's execution states differ from the original at assertion points — directly encoding the information most relevant to the correct/overfitting verdict.

The design is motivated by an information-theoretic argument: verdict tasks have O(1) output entropy (1 bit for binary, log₂k bits for k-way classification), so the trace should contain only the information needed to determine that output, not the full O(n) execution simulation.
